headline: An AI rebound lifted stocks Wednesday, but Nvidia's leadership turmoil after the bell and roughly 91% odds of a December Fed hike set a shakier tone for Thursday.
dateline: Thursday, November 12, 2026 · closes as of Wed Nov 11

rundown.h: December hike odds climb to about 91%.
rundown.p: Futures now price roughly a 91% chance the Fed raises rates in December, up from 84% Tuesday and about 74% a week ago, Trading Economics said Thursday; the 10-year Treasury yield traded near 5.00%. PIMCO's baseline is a December hike, with the risk of one more early in 2027. Thursday is the first cash Treasury session since the hot CPI, after the Veterans Day close.

rundown.h: Nvidia's board drama hits after hours.
rundown.p: Nvidia shares fell as much as 10% after Wednesday's close after the Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang, and the New York Times reported allegations involving Huang and an executive, per Trading Economics. The board opened an independent probe Nov. 8. Nasdaq 100 futures were down about 0.9% early Thursday: Nvidia is the AI trade's bellwether, and its results are due within days.

rundown.h: Small-business owners hold steady, and grumble about taxes.
rundown.p: The NFIB optimism index edged down to 97.8 in October from 97.9, its lowest since June and just above the 97.7 forecast. Labor quality stayed the top problem at 25%, but 21% of owners named taxes, the highest since May 2021. A net 8% expect better conditions in six months, up 2 points. Main Street isn't cracking, but it isn't hiring with gusto either.

The AI developer filed for an estimated $75 billion Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT, with $19.7 billion of revenue in the 12 months to June 30, Renaissance Capital said; pricing could come the week of Nov. 16. Reports describe the book as oversubscribed at a targeted $1.5 trillion valuation. It would match SpaceX's $75 billion June raise, a fresh test of appetite for AI paper with yields near 5%.
rundown.src: Renaissance Capital · Oct 26; Trading Economics · Nov 11

rundown.h: OPEC pumped nearly 2 million more barrels a day.
rundown.p: OPEC crude output rose almost 2 million barrels a day in October to 27.16 million, ING said, with Saudi Arabia reporting production near prewar levels. The API also reported a 9-million-barrel U.S. crude build for the week to Nov. 6. More supply is the main thing keeping a lid on crude, and eventually diesel, the fuel that sets trucking costs.

dive.title: The warehouse glut is gone. The next one is being poured.
dive.dek: Record leasing has pulled industrial vacancy off its peak, and developers are already breaking ground again.
body: Two years ago the story in warehouses was oversupply: the 2021–22 building boom delivered space faster than tenants could fill it. That story is over. Cushman & Wakefield put national industrial vacancy at 6.8% in the third quarter, 20 basis points below its late-2025 peak and the lowest since the end of 2024 (Oct. 12). CBRE, which measures differently, has it at 6.4%, down 20 basis points from a year earlier (Oct. 23).

Demand did the work. CBRE counted 104.6 million square feet of net absorption in the quarter, the most since late 2022 and well above its 10-year quarterly average of 82.9 million. Leasing hit 276.8 million square feet, up 27.1% from a year earlier, and Savills says the second and third quarters together were the strongest two-quarter stretch it has on record. Meanwhile supply fell: high rates froze starts in 2023–25, so completions through September were down 17% year over year by CBRE's count.

Developers noticed. Cushman counts about 324 million square feet under construction, up 23% from a year earlier, roughly a third of it build-to-suit; CBRE (278 million, +9.3%) and Savills (321.6 million, +10.2%) agree on the direction. Rents are rising but not racing: CBRE's average asking rent is $11.16 a foot, up 3.6%, roughly flat after inflation. And the recovery is lopsided. Savills data, via Propmodo, show big boxes tightening while Class B and C space has lost occupancy for 13 straight quarters, and Inland Empire rents are down 11.6% in a year.

Why it matters: industrial remains the healthiest corner of commercial real estate, but a new pipeline is now chasing a leasing boom that may have been pulled forward. What would change the picture: if rates stay near 5%, speculative starts get harder to finance, which protects owners of existing buildings. If demand cools in 2027 just as this space delivers, vacancy turns back up, starting in the Sunbelt markets where building is busiest.
watch: Early December: Census October construction spending, a read on new building.
Mid-to-late January: Q4 broker reports; do starts keep climbing?
Where the 10-year settles after the Dec. 8–9 Fed meeting, the swing factor for spec financing.

items.title: October LMI: inventory costs hit their highest since March 2022 as firms stocked up
body: The Logistics Managers' Index rose to 70.7 in October from 70.2 in September, the second-strongest reading in four years behind June's 71.1, according to the Nov. 3 release. Readings above 50 signal expansion; the index averaged 62.2 from 2016 to 2026 and slipped to 66.6 in August before rebounding.

Costs drove the gain. Inventory costs jumped to 88.8 from 79.9, the highest since March 2022, as inventory levels rose to 66.9 from 58.9. Warehousing prices climbed to 80.7 from 73.5 while warehousing capacity stayed in contraction at 43.5. Aggregate logistics costs reached 257.5, up 11.4 points and the fastest expansion since March 2022.

Transportation prices eased to 88 from 92.7 but remained well into expansion, with transportation capacity still contracting at 38. The release came a week before October CPI, which showed core prices rising 0.3%.

lead.title: Iran calls the Qatar talks 'lies' as mines disable two more supertankers
lead.body:
Tehran slammed the diplomatic door, at least in public. On Nov. 11 Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's security council, called reports of a U.S.–Iran meeting in Qatar "pure lies" meant to push oil prices down; President Pezeshkian accused Washington of diplomacy by threat, and Secretary of State Rubio rejected Iran's demand for war reparations (Oilprice.com). On Nov. 12 Rezaei said Iran will not let any enriched nuclear material leave the country (Reuters, via Engine).

At sea, two supertankers were disabled by explosions in the strait Wednesday night; the IRGC Navy said they ignored warnings about an "unauthorized route," and Iranian state media said they hit mines (Cornerstone Futures). The Washington Institute counted 37 ships struck in October, the most of any month of the war, and Allianz Trade puts physical damage across the Gulf above $200 billion.
lead.reach: Through oil: Brent settled up 1.39% at $92.76 on Nov. 11 as Iran denied the talks, yet it is still down about 21% since November began on bets the war is winding down (Oilprice.com, Nov 11). Each flare-up feeds fuel, freight and inflation expectations, and with them Treasury yields.

views.view: Reads oil's rebound as fading hope for an imminent de-escalation.
Calls Brent near $90 an oddity: too low if the war escalates, too high if a deal is signed.

reading.title: Invest in what you know, then do the homework
reading.dek: Peter Lynch's best-known slogan was meant as the place research starts, and his six stock categories are the tool he used to carry it through.
body: Between 1977 and 1990, Peter Lynch ran Fidelity's Magellan Fund and oversaw its growth from $18 million to more than $14 billion in assets while posting an average annual return of 29.2%. Yet the idea he is best remembered for sounds almost homespun: invest in what you know. In One Up on Wall Street (1989), written with John Rothchild, he argued that ordinary people often notice a great business at the mall, at work, or in their own kitchen long before analysts do.

But the slogan is routinely misread. Lynch did not mean that liking a product is reason enough to buy the stock. Familiarity is where research begins, not where it ends. A popular store or gadget earns a company a spot on your watch list; whether it earns a spot in your portfolio depends on the balance sheet, the earnings trend and, crucially, the price. Pay too much for even a wonderful company and the business can do everything right while the stock goes nowhere.

His framework for that homework starts with sorting. Lynch placed stocks into six buckets: slow growers, mature firms held mainly for dividends; stalwarts, large companies growing somewhat faster than the economy; fast growers, smaller firms expanding rapidly, with the most upside and the most risk; cyclicals, whose profits rise and fall with the economy; turnarounds, troubled companies with a plausible path back; and asset plays, businesses sitting on assets the market undervalues. Each category comes with different expectations and different warning signs. You would not expect a stalwart to triple, nor hold a cyclical forever.

Sorting forces a discipline Lynch prized: being able to explain, in a few plain sentences, why you own something and what would have to happen for the investment to work. He suggested picking a story line and checking whether the company keeps following it. If you cannot tell that story, you are likely relying on momentum or someone else's conviction, and you will have little to steady you when the price drops for reasons unrelated to the business.

That test matters more when indexes sit near records and leadership is concentrated in a handful of AI-linked giants. Many investors own those companies through funds without ever classifying them. Is a given chip or cloud name a stalwart, a fast grower, or something closer to a cyclical riding a spending boom? The answer shapes what valuation is reasonable and what news should worry you. With the 10-year Treasury yielding near 5%, a stock now has to earn its place against a credible risk-free alternative.

quote.text: Know what you own, and know why you own it.
quote.src: Peter Lynch, One Up on Wall Street (1989)

takeaways: Classify each AI holding: stalwart, fast grower or cyclical? The label sets the valuation.
With 10-year yields near 5%, demand a clear earnings story before paying record prices.
A December hike may jolt prices; owners who know their story can hold steady.
